Will Logseq render relative markdown links? What about if a page is renamed, will it refactor relative markdown links to that page?

Short answer: No for page-to-page relative markdown like [label](./Other.md). Logseq does not treat filesystem-relative .md paths as graph page links. Rename refactoring also does not update those paths — only tracked page refs ([[Page]], and related #tags / properties Logseq indexes) get rewritten when you rename a page.
Will Logseq render relative markdown links? What about if a page is renamed, will it refactor relative markdown links to that page?
Will Logseq render relative markdown links? What about if a page is renamed, will it refactor relative markdown links to that page?
Official page linking is wiki-style: [[page name]], or labeled [display text]([[page name]]). External URLs use ordinary [label](https://…) markdown. Answer/Official from Logseq docs — Markdown.
Will Logseq render relative markdown links? What about if a page is renamed, will it refactor relative markdown links to that page?
Relative links to assets do render (e.g. ![img](../assets/foo.png)). That is file/media linking, not page linking.
Will Logseq render relative markdown links? What about if a page is renamed, will it refactor relative markdown links to that page?

Relative links to other pages as files — [label](Other.md), [label](./pages/Other.md) — are not resolved to the existing page. A collaborator stated there is no “local markdown” page model: pages are flat by basename, and relative paths are incompatible with that design. Clicking such a link can open/create the wrong page (often from the link label), rather than navigating to the target file. Answer/Official from Discussion #8003 (incl. follow-up that relative local links were “not on the radar” as of 2023).
Will Logseq render relative markdown links? What about if a page is renamed, will it refactor relative markdown links to that page?
Will Logseq render relative markdown links? What about if a page is renamed, will it refactor relative markdown links to that page?

Renaming a page in Logseq rewrites page references elsewhere in the graph ([[Old Name]] → [[New Name]], and most #tag / property refs Logseq tracks). That refactor walks blocks that reference the page in the DB — not arbitrary markdown path strings.
Will Logseq render relative markdown links? What about if a page is renamed, will it refactor relative markdown links to that page?

A relative [label](./Old.md) (or similar) is not a page reference, so rename will not rewrite it. Even labeled markdown forms that target a page title without [[…]] are weaker than wikilinks for rename/display behavior; prefer [[Page]] or [label]([[Page]]) for links you want to survive renames.

Will Logseq render relative markdown links? What about if a page is renamed, will it refactor relative markdown links to that page?

Use [[wikilinks]] (or [label]([[Page]])) for inter-page links in Logseq. Use relative markdown only for assets/media. Do not rely on Obsidian/GitHub-style [text](./sibling.md) paths for graph navigation or rename safety.

Lifestyles of Health and Sustainability — a market segment of consumers who choose products and services for their personal health, their environmental impact and their social values.

LOHAS is a marketing term for a kind of customer. It covers people who buy organic food, natural personal care, green building materials, renewable energy, eco-tourism, yoga and alternative medicine, and who want products "of equal quality" that are "also virtuous," in sociologist Paul H. Ray's phrase.
Gaiam sorted the market into five segments: sustainable economy, healthy living, alternative health, personal development and ecological living.
1994 — Paul H. Ray begins a national survey of American values.

1996 — Ray names a values cluster he calls the "Cultural Creatives": people who carried the 1960s concerns with ecology, peace and human rights into their everyday choices. He counted them at about a quarter of American adults.
2000 — Ray and Sherry Ruth Anderson publish The Cultural Creatives: How 50 Million People Are Changing the World.

Late 1990s — journalists Frank Lampe and Steven Hoffman connect the Cultural Creatives to the booming natural and organic products market. Their company, Natural Business Communications, coins "LOHAS" as a trade term, researches the segment with Ray, and publishes the Natural Business LOHAS Journal.
1998–1999 — Jirka Rysavy's Gaiam buys complementary businesses such as Living Arts and InnerBalance Health to build one trusted brand across the LOHAS market.
2006 — the Worldwatch Institute puts the LOHAS market at about $300 billion, roughly 30% of U.S. consumer spending.
2007 — Natural Marketing Institute research counts about 41 million Americans, 13% of the population, as LOHAS consumers. In Japan about 17 million adults, 12% of the population, fit the segment.

Lua is a small, embeddable, dynamically typed programming language designed to be easy to integrate into larger applications.
Created in 1993 at PUC-Rio in Brazil by Roberto Ierusalimschy, Waldemar Celes, and Luiz Henrique de Figueiredo.
It was designed in part as a lightweight extension language that host programs could embed without taking on a large runtime.
Gives applications a compact scripting language for configuration, automation, and extension.
Works well when the host system wants users to customize behavior without exposing the whole implementation language.
Fits environments where a small runtime, simple C API, and portability matter.
Embedding inside tools, games, editors, and music devices.
Scripting and extension points where startup cost and implementation size matter.
Data-table-oriented programming with a relatively small core language.
Large codebases that need strong static guarantees by default.
Complex package-management and tooling workflows compared with larger ecosystems.
Readability and maintainability when code leans too heavily on dynamic patterns and table metaprogramming.
Often shows up in nvim configuration and embedded scripting environments like Monome/Norns.
